'''''Leucospermum truncatum''''', commonly known as the '''limestone pincushion''', is a shrub native to South Africa. The flowers are initially bright yellow but turn orange with time. Flowers can be found between August and December.

== Description ==
''Leucospermum truncatum'' is a rounded, upright, well-branched shrub of up to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} high, with a single main stem at its foot, covered in minute soft crinkly hairs. Its simple long spade-shaped leaves are set [[Leaf#Arrangement on the stem|alternately]], have a squared-off end, mostly with three (sometimes non, five or seven) blunt teeth with a rounded bony tip, {{convert|4.5–9|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, and {{convert|8–15|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide. The flowering stems are stiffly upright and {{convert|1/2|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name=Rourke />

The flower heads are globe-shaped, usually with two or three together and sit on a stalk of up to {{convert|2|cm|in|abbr=on}} long. Each flowerhead of {{convert|3|–|4|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter. The [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] is yellow in colour, {{convert|18–35|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, straight or slightly bend towards the center of the flower head. The [[pollen-presenter]], a thickening at the tip of the style (comparable with the "head" of the pin), is cylindric in shape with a blunt end, {{convert|1–2|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, initially carrying bright yellow [[pollen]]. The [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]] is a transverse groove at the very tip of the pollen-presenter. At the base of the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] are four linear, so-called hypogynous scales of about {{convert|1|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Rourke />

The subtribe Proteinae, to which the genus ''Leucospermum'' has been assigned, consistently has a basic chromosome number of twelve ([[Diploid|2n]]=24).<ref>{{cite journal|first1= L.A.S.|last1= Johnson|first2= Barbara G.|last2= Briggs|year= 1975|title= On the Proteaceae—the evolution and classification of a southern family|journal= Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|volume= 70|issue= 2|page= 106|doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.1975.tb01644.x}}{{Dead link|date=February 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The name ''Leucospermum truncatum'' was first used in 1843 by [[Heinrich Wilhelm Buek]] for a specimen that was collected by [[Johann Franz Drège]] in August 1831, just east of [[Cape Agulhas]] on a limestone hill. He however failed to add a description, and therefore ''L. truncatum'' <small>H.Buek</small> is a [[nomen nudum]]. In 1856, [[Carl Meissner]] used Buek's [[epithet]] for ''Leucospermum zeyheri'' [[var.]] ''truncatum'', adding the necessary description in Latin. [[Otto Kuntze]] moved ''truncatum'' in 1891 to ''Leucadendron''. [[John Patrick Rourke]] in 1967, raised Meissner's variety to a separate species and made the [[new combination]] ''Leucospermum truncatum''.<ref name=Rourke />

== Distribution, habitat and ecology == 
''Leucospermum truncatum'' grows in [[fynbos]] on the limestone ridge close to the coast from sea level to {{convert|240|m|ft|abbr=on}} elevation, between [[Soetanysberg]] in the west, across the [[Bredasdorp]] district, to [[Vermaaklikheid]]. It can only be found on deposits of the [[Alexandria Formation]]. The roots of the plants often penetrate crevices in pure limestone outcrops. The species forms open thickets with ''[[Protea obtusifolia]]'', ''[[Leucadendron meridianum]]'' and ''[[Leucadendron muirii]]''. The average rainfall in the range of the limestone pincushion is about {{convert|40–50|cm|in|abbr=on}} per year, most of which falls during the winter.<ref name=Rourke /> The flowerheads are primarily pollinated by birds. The seeds are released from the fruit about two months after flowering and are collected by ants that store them underground (a seed dispersal strategy that is called [[myrmecochory]]).<ref>{{cite web|website= Protea Atlas Project|title= Wide-tubed Pincushions - Leucospermum|url= https://www.proteaatlas.org.za/pincush2.htm}}</ref> These plants rarely survive the fires that naturally occur every decade or two in the fynbos. When afterwards the rain carries specific chemicals that are created by the fire underground, the seeds germinate and the species is so "resurrected".
